article.title: Fitzpatrick Skin Type Test: 6-Question Quiz & Type Guide
article.meta_description: Take a quick Fitzpatrick skin type test, learn what types I to VI mean, and see how the scale differs from skin tone and undertone for makeup and color.
article.h1: Fitzpatrick Skin Type Test: A 6-Question Quiz and Guide to Types I–VI
article.body_html:
A Fitzpatrick skin type test sorts you into one of six types (I to VI) based on your natural coloring and how your skin usually reacts to unprotected sun. The quick quiz below gives you a rough self-estimate in a couple of minutes. It then explains what each type means and what it can't tell you. It is general education, not a medical assessment, and it is not a way to pick makeup shades.

What the Fitzpatrick scale is (and what it isn't)

A six-type grouping based on how skin typically reacts to sun

The Fitzpatrick scale was developed in the 1970s by dermatologist Thomas Fitzpatrick. It groups people by their typical reaction to sun exposure, such as burning, tanning, or both. Type I is the group that burns most easily and tans least. Type VI is the group with the most natural pigmentation, which burns least readily. It is a broad grouping, so plenty of people sit between two types.

Why it is not the same as skin tone, undertone, or oily/dry skin type

People often mix these terms up, but they describe different things. Fitzpatrick type is about sun reaction. Skin tone (depth) is how light or deep your skin looks. Undertone is the cool, warm, neutral, or olive tint beneath the surface. Oily, dry, and combination describe skin texture and oil balance, which is a separate topic again.

A self-test is a rough estimate, not a clinical assessment

A home quiz relies on your memory and your own judgment. A clinician can ask more detailed questions and look at your skin directly. Use your result as shared vocabulary and a talking point, not as a verdict.

Before you start: how to answer fairly

  • Think about skin that rarely sees the sun, such as the inner upper arm or the underside of the wrist, not your face or hands.
  • Answer from your natural coloring. Ignore tans, self-tanner, and hair dye. If your hair is colored, think about what it was in childhood.
  • Go with your usual reaction, not your best or worst day. If you can't remember, pick the answer that fits most summers.

The Fitzpatrick skin type test: 6 quick questions

This is a simplified version made for orientation. Note the points next to the answer that fits you best. Questions 1 to 4 are about natural coloring. Questions 5 and 6 are about sun reaction, which is what the scale is really built on, so those two count double in the scoring step.

Question 1: Natural eye color

  • Very pale or icy blue, gray, or green: 0
  • Medium or deeper blue, gray, or green: 1
  • Hazel or light brown: 2
  • Dark brown: 3
  • Brownish black: 4

Question 2: Natural hair color

  • Red or very light blond: 0
  • Blond: 1
  • Dark blond or light brown: 2
  • Dark brown: 3
  • Black: 4

Question 3: Natural skin color in unexposed areas

  • Ivory or very pale: 0
  • Pale or fair: 1
  • Beige or light olive: 2
  • Medium brown or olive: 3
  • Dark brown or deeper: 4

Question 4: Freckling

  • Many freckles: 0
  • Several: 1
  • A few: 2
  • Very few: 3
  • None: 4

Question 5: What usually happens after sun exposure without protection

  • Always burns, with painful redness and peeling: 0
  • Usually burns and peels: 1
  • Sometimes a mild burn: 2
  • Rarely burns: 3
  • Almost never visibly burns: 4

Question 6: How easily you tan afterward

  • Never tans, only turns red: 0
  • Tans lightly and with difficulty: 1
  • Tans gradually to light brown: 2
  • Tans easily to medium brown: 3
  • Tans very easily to deep brown: 4

Add up your answers: Fitzpatrick types I–VI explained

How to score the quiz and match it to a type

Add your points for Questions 1 to 4. Then add your points for Questions 5 and 6 and double that sum. Your total will be between 0 and 32. Match it to this range:

  • 0–5: Type I
  • 6–10: Type II
  • 11–16: Type III
  • 17–21: Type IV
  • 22–26: Type V
  • 27–32: Type VI

These cutoffs are my own simplification for a quick self-estimate. They are not an official clinical scoring tool, and the bands are not perfectly equal in width. Because several questions are about coloring, someone with very pale skin and no freckles can land a type higher than their real sun reaction suggests. If your total seems off, give extra weight to Questions 5 and 6.

Types I and II: typically very fair to fair skin that tends to burn easily

Type I usually means very pale skin, often with light eyes, light or red hair, and freckles, that burns quickly and rarely tans. Type II is similar but may tan a little with time. Both have a strong, fast reaction to sun.

Types III and IV: typically medium to olive or light brown skin with a more mixed reaction

Type III often burns at first and then tans gradually. Type IV burns less often and tans more easily, and is common among people with olive or light brown skin. Reactions in these groups vary widely from person to person.

Types V and VI: typically brown to deeply pigmented skin that burns less readily

Type V usually has brown skin that rarely burns and tans easily. Type VI has deeply pigmented skin that almost never visibly burns. "Burns less readily" does not mean "never affected by the sun," so sun protection still matters (more on that below).

If you land between two types

This is common, especially near a cutoff like 10 and 11. Read both descriptions and pick the one that matches your actual sun reactions, which is why Questions 5 and 6 count double. The scale is a coarse grouping, so treat the result as a range, not an exact label. A dermatologist is the right person to ask if you want a firm answer.

Fitzpatrick type vs skin tone vs undertone

A simple comparison

TermWhat it describesTypically used for
Fitzpatrick typeHow skin usually reacts to sun, in six groupsGeneral context and conversations about sun reaction
Skin tone (depth)How light or deep your skin looksFoundation depth, overall color contrast
UndertoneCool, warm, neutral, or olive tint beneath the surfaceChoosing flattering makeup and clothing colors

Why two people with the same Fitzpatrick type can need very different foundation shades

Say two people both score as Type III. One has a golden, warm undertone and looks best in camel, olive green, and coral lipstick. The other has a cool, rosy undertone and looks better in navy, plum, and rose. The scale puts them in the same group but says nothing about those differences.

Link to our skin tone and undertone guides

For makeup and color choices, work out your depth and undertone instead. Our guides on finding your skin tone depth and undertone and simple undertone tests walk through it step by step.

What your result is and isn't useful for

Useful as general context

Your type gives you shared language when you talk to a clinician, aesthetician, or anyone else who uses the scale. It can also help you reflect on how your skin has reacted to sun in the past.

Not a way to pick a foundation shade or a lipstick color

The scale has only six groups. Foundation ranges have many more shades, split by depth and undertone. Two people in the same Fitzpatrick type can sit at opposite ends of a brand's range.

Why every skin type needs sun protection

No type is exempt. A higher type number does not mean you can skip sunscreen. Everyone benefits from sun protection, and a doctor can advise on what suits you.

Using your results for color and makeup choices

Start with depth and undertone

Once you know your depth and undertone, put them to work. A warm undertone often suits cream, camel, olive, and rust with gold jewelry, for example a camel coat over a cream knit. A cool undertone often suits navy, charcoal, and berry with silver jewelry, such as a navy blazer over a white tee.

Use natural contrast and personal preference as the final filter

If your hair, eyes, and skin are high contrast, bold pairings like black with white tend to work. If they are softer, tonal outfits such as stone with oatmeal often feel more balanced. If you love a color that "shouldn't" suit you, wear it away from your face or add a scarf or necklace in a friendlier shade.

Test shades in daylight at the jawline

For foundation, swipe two or three close shades along the jawline and check them in natural light. The one that blends into your neck and face is the one to take home.

Where an app can fit in (and where it can't)

What a camera-based cosmetic overview can offer

FitCheck: AI Outfit Planner, free on Google Play for Android, includes a live skin analysis that uses your camera to give an AI skin overview with cosmetic beauty suggestions. It can be a starting point once you're thinking about makeup and color. The app also offers live virtual makeup try-on, so you can preview looks such as lipstick on your own face. For makeup try-on, face natural light, hold the camera at eye level, and avoid filters.

Why it does not determine your Fitzpatrick type or sun sensitivity

The app doesn't determine a Fitzpatrick type or measure how your skin reacts to sun. A photo can't show how your skin has responded to sun over the years, and that history is what the scale is built on.

Treat AI feedback as a second opinion

The feedback is an AI opinion, not a professional assessment. Use it as a prompt for experimenting, and trust your own eye and comfort in the end.

Not medical advice: when to see a dermatologist

This quiz and any AI tool are cosmetic, not medical

This article and its quiz are cosmetic and educational. AI feedback, including from any app, is not medical advice, and you should see a dermatologist or doctor for any skin concern.

See a professional for changes or worries

Book an appointment if you notice a new or changing spot on your skin, or anything else that worries you. Don't wait for a quiz or an app to tell you it's fine.

Ask about sun protection for your situation

A doctor or dermatologist can advise on sunscreen and sun habits based on your own history. That advice is worth more than any general quiz result.

faqs.question: Is the Fitzpatrick scale accurate?
faqs.answer: It is a useful broad grouping, but it is not precise. It sorts people into just six categories, and many people fit between two. A home quiz depends on your own recollection, so treat the result as a rough estimate rather than a clinical finding.

faqs.question: Is Fitzpatrick type the same as skin tone?
faqs.answer: No. Fitzpatrick type describes how skin typically reacts to sun, while skin tone describes how light or deep your skin looks, and undertone is the cool, warm, neutral, or olive tint beneath the surface. Two people with the same type can have quite different tones and undertones.

faqs.question: Does my Fitzpatrick type tell me which foundation to buy?
faqs.answer: Not really. Foundation shades are matched by depth and undertone, and six groups are too broad for that. Test a few close shades along your jawline in daylight instead.

faqs.question: Can I skip sunscreen with a higher Fitzpatrick type?
faqs.answer: No. People of every skin type benefit from sun protection, even if their skin burns less readily. Ask a doctor or dermatologist what is right for you.

faqs.question: Can an app tell me my Fitzpatrick type?
faqs.answer: A photo can't show how your skin reacts to sun over time, so an app shouldn't be treated as a way to find your type. FitCheck's live skin analysis gives a cosmetic overview with beauty suggestions and does not determine a Fitzpatrick type or sun sensitivity. It is not medical advice.

review.notes: The article matches informational intent: it gives a working quiz, scoring and type descriptions, and it separates Fitzpatrick type from skin tone and undertone. The scoring arithmetic checks out (Q1-4 max 16, plus doubled Q5-6 max 16, giving 0-32, and the bands cover that range with no gaps). The cutoffs are disclosed as the author's own simplification, not a clinical tool. The quiz is loosely modeled on the original Fitzpatrick questionnaire, which uses different questions and bands, so some readers may expect those. Consider a short line saying so. The app claims stay within APP_FACTS: free on Google Play for Android, live skin analysis described as cosmetic, live virtual makeup try-on, and the photo tips. It explicitly says the app does not determine a Fitzpatrick type, and it makes no medical, accuracy, storage or privacy claims. Dermatologist referrals and the 'not medical advice' text are appropriate. The color and styling advice is conventional and sound. Minor: the intro says the quiz is 'not a way to pick makeup shades', yet a later section is titled 'Using your results for color and makeup choices'. It then correctly redirects to depth and undertone, so retitling it 'Using depth and undertone' would be clearer. The app section is short and does not push the app too hard. The internal links should be checked to make sure they resolve.
